title: Korach: sounds fair (Numbers 16:3)
hookLine: Korach says all the congregation is holy; the words are true, the motive is not

lines: A SPEECH MADE OF TRUE SENTENCES.
cards: A speech can be built entirely out of true sentences. Everyone deserves a voice. The people in charge have been there too long.
Why should a few decide for everyone? A listener can agree with every word and still sense something off, once they notice who's speaking, and what that person would get if they won.
This week's portion opens with exactly that kind of speech, delivered to Moses' face, in front of a crowd, by his own cousin. And the line at the center of it is hard to argue with.

teach.b: Korach is a Levite, a grandson of Kohath, from the same family as Moses and Aaron.

He gathers Dathan and Abiram, and two hundred fifty respected leaders, and they confront Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them; wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"
Every phrase has a source. At Sinai, God called the whole people a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. In Leviticus, holiness was spoken to the whole congregation.
Korach echoes the Torah back at Moses. So what's wrong? The rabbis looked under the speech.
Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says Korach was jealous: a younger cousin had been appointed leader of their clan instead of him. A midrash pictures his opening move.
He dresses his followers in cloaks made entirely of blue wool and asks Moses: does a cloak that's all blue still need a blue thread in its fringes? Moses says yes. Korach's crowd laughs.
He's using yesterday's commandment to make both the law and Moses look ridiculous. Then Moses answers, and exposes the motive. You Levites, he says, isn't it enough that you serve at the sanctuary?

teach.h: NOW YOU WANT THE PRIESTHOOD TOO?
teach.b: Now you want the priesthood too?
He even hands Korach's words back: you take too much upon you. In the rabbis' reading, the claim was that everyone is equal. The goal was to be above.

how: When the portion Korach is read, Jewish teachers often pair Korach's speech with the midrash of the all-blue cloak, and use it to talk about the difference between a true claim and the reason someone is making it.

o: the younger cousin made leader of the clan
the blue thread worn in the corner fringes
the Levite who rebelled against Moses and Aaron

games.q: the rebel's speech — tap the pairs.
p: now you want the priesthood too?

s: Korach's claim that all the people are holy has no basis in the Torah
at Sinai the people are called a holy nation; his words echo the Torah.
Rashi says Korach was jealous of a cousin's appointment
a younger cousin was made leader of their clan.
Moses used Korach's own phrase against him
you take too much upon you, Moses says back.

games.q: you're Moses. Korach's crowd wears cloaks all of blue and asks: does a cloak that's entirely blue still need a blue thread in its fringes? what do you answer?
games.why: in the midrash Moses says yes, and Korach's crowd laughs. the question was built to make the law look silly, not to learn it.

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now, at work, at home, online, and say your position to yourself in its best words.
Then ask quietly what you'd get if you won: respect, being right, a seat you've wanted, an old score settled? Don't judge what you find; just notice whether the words and the want point the same way.

wordCard.voice: Korach. The Levite who said all the congregation is holy, true words, carried by a wish to be above them.

orig.note: Hebrew: you take too much upon you. Korach's charge, and Moses' answer back.

carryVoice: Your line: what's under the argument. True words can still carry a want. That's day four hundred fifty-one.
